items.gist: Defines piṇḍastha as the yogin's adhiṣṭheya samāpatti and its relation to piṇḍa. It sets up the state in which the yogin is established in the object.
Describes the jñānin's sarvatobhadra fullness and the three names arising from lokayoga and prasaṃkhyāna. The same pattern applies in svapna and related states.
Explains the vedya established in adhiṣṭhāna and distinguishes clear waking from svapna. Svapna arises when the vedya is less distinct or internally imagined.
Presents fourfold variations and names them laukika svapna. It also describes svapna as pervasion and the yogin's independence from external vedya-sattā.
Identifies vedya-chāya as the adhiṣṭhāna and the seed-state of the universe as sauṣupta. The sleeper's non-grasping of bhāvas is likened to ordinary sleep.
Explains rūpastha through samāpatti and udāsīnya, then the fourfold vedya. Turya is śaktisamāveśa beyond ordinary udāsīnya.
Describes saṃvitsvaprakāśā and the triad of meya, māna, and mātṛ. Pramātṛtā is svatantratva, and samāveśa clarifies the threefold structure.
States that jāgrat and other states are established as śakti. It distinguishes parā śakti and says turyadaśā has no further aparā state.
Defines turyātīta as full, unbounded ānanda and the supreme padam. It denies yoga there and emphasizes satatodita all-pervasiveness.
Rejects the confused view and identifies Śiva as niṣprapañca, nirābhāsa, and all-transcendent. Knowing him brings liberation.
Introduces another account of jāgrat and svapna. In turya stand mantratannātha and adhīśvara, while bhāvas become self-nondual.
Describes bhāvas losing their own essence and entering turyātīta. It distinguishes stable waking, unstable svapna, and indistinct supta, with turya as their thread.
Maps layākala's own form to waking and svapna in sequence. It equates jñānaśakti with svapna, kriyāśakti with jāgrat, and says all is ultimately there.
